newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: SCHIPHOL USERS TO FIGHT NIGHT FLIGHT BAN IN COURT.
newsitem.headline: SCHIPHOL USERS TO FIGHT NIGHT FLIGHT BAN IN COURT.

text.p: Dutch Air Transport Association (ATAN) said on Thursday it was joining the legal battle to overturn a ban on night flights at Amsterdam's Schiphol Airport.

The air freight sector association said it will seek a court injunction against Schiphol and the Dutch state to suspend the ban on night-time flights by wide-body aircraft and to tolerate the resultant increase in noise above legal annual limits.

"At the very least we are demanding the ban be suspended until December 31 to give all airlines involved the opportunity to make the necessary adjustments to their schedules," ATAN spokesman Hans Knuvers said.

Knuvers said the case, brought together with cargo handler Aero Ground Services and Israeli airline El Al, would be heard simultaneously with charter airline Martinair's suit, aimed at gaining an exemption from the ban for its Boeing 747 flights.
Martinair announced earlier its application to overturn the ban would be heard at 1100 GMT on Friday.
El Al said previously it may transfer its freight hub to Liege in Belgium if the ban is upheld.
"ATAN is of the view that the (night restriction) measures not only run counter to the policy of expanding Schiphol into a European mainport but actually make it impossible," ATAN said.
"Not only ATAN members, but the entire private sector and Dutch society as a whole will suffer exceptional (economic) damage," the association's statement added.

The night flight ban, aimed at keeping noise levels at Schiphol within legal limits imposed this year for the first time, particularly affects the freight sector, and to a lesser extent passenger charters.
The ban prohibits take-offs of most wide-body aircraft and any unscheduled flights between 2300 and 0600 hours local time.
ATAN said the debate on noise levels had so far failed to take account of the economic implications of reduced freight flows into the airport.
Directly and indirectly the air freight sector provided some 75,000 jobs and contributed an annual 9.3 billion guilders ($4.4 billion) to the economy or 1.6 percent of gross added value, it said.
The noise reduction measures would be harmful both in the short and medium term, it said.
Aero Ground Services, Schiphol's single biggest independent cargo handler looked set to lose some 50 percent of its freight volume in the very short term, it added.
This would have "disastrous consequences" for Aero's 100 staff, it cautioned.
